title: Visuospatial Neglect - a Theory-Informed Overview of Current and Emerging Strategies and a Systematic Review on the Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Clinical Phenomenology of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definition, Differential Diagnosis, and Core Presentations
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is a heterogeneous neuropsychological syndrome in which patients fail to orient, respond, or act toward stimuli on the side contralesional to a brain lesion, most commonly after right-hemisphere stroke, despite preserved primary sensory pathways. Clinically, it is better understood as a disorder of spatial attention and action than as a simple perceptual loss, and it may affect exploratory behavior, object-centered processing, personal space, and motor output to different degrees. This heterogeneity explains why bedside detection requires convergent assessment across cancellation, line bisection, copying, reading, and observation of spontaneous behavior rather than reliance on a single task [1].

A central differential-diagnostic issue is distinguishing neglect from homonymous hemianopia. Although both can produce failures to report contralesional events, hemianopia reflects a sensory field defect, whereas neglect is characterized by impaired exploration and reduced awareness or use of contralesional space that may extend beyond the visual modality; double dissociations and partial overlap are well documented, making careful clinical examination essential [1]. Neglect must also be separated from related but distinct disorders of action and awareness, including motor neglect and anosognosia for hemiplegia. Motor neglect refers to underutilization of the contralesional limb not fully explained by weakness, often accompanied by impaired spontaneous bimanual coordination, while anosognosia concerns lack of awareness of paralysis; these syndromes may co-occur but can dissociate, underscoring the multidimensional structure of neglect-related disorders [2,3,4].

Core presentations therefore include perceptual-attentional neglect, premotor or intentional neglect, and reduced awareness of contralesional events, often expressed in everyday acts such as eating from one side of the plate, grooming only one side of the body, colliding with obstacles, or omitting left-sided elements in drawing and reading. Contemporary accounts emphasize that neglect is not a unitary entity but a family of spatially lateralized deficits spanning input, internal representation, and output domains, a distinction with major implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection [3,4].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Clinical Phenomenology of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology, Laterality, and Outcome Relevance
subsections.content:
Reported prevalence of visuospatial neglect after stroke varies widely, largely because estimates depend on sampling frame (acute versus rehabilitation cohorts), lesion side, neglect subtype assessed, and the sensitivity and number of tests applied. Methodological reviews have therefore emphasized that apparent epidemiological inconsistency is often measurement-driven rather than biologically contradictory ref [8]. In acute stroke cohorts, neglect is among the most common cognitive-attentional syndromes, with substantial early incidence and a course characterized by partial spontaneous improvement over weeks to months, although a clinically meaningful minority remains impaired beyond the hyperacute phase ref [6].

Laterality is a central but sometimes oversimplified issue. Neglect is more frequent and typically more severe after right hemisphere stroke, contributing to the classic predominance of left-sided neglect in clinical series ref [6]. However, rightward neglect after left hemisphere damage is well documented when assessed carefully, including in quantitative studies showing that left hemisphere lesions can produce genuine, if often milder or more transient, spatial bias ref [10]. Related asymmetries are also seen for extinction, which has been reported more often after right than left hemisphere stroke ref [9]. Epidemiological interpretation is further complicated by ascertainment bias, since left-sided motor and language-dominant presentations may facilitate recognition of some strokes, whereas right hemisphere syndromes can be underdetected in routine care ref [5].

Outcome relevance is considerable. Neglect predicts poorer functional status, reduced independence in activities of daily living, prolonged rehabilitation needs, and less favorable discharge disposition beyond the effect of motor deficit alone ref [7]. In cohort studies, its presence has also been associated with larger lesions and with slower or incomplete recovery trajectories ref [6]. These observations make neglect not merely an epiphenomenon of stroke severity, but a clinically consequential disorder whose detection is essential for prognosis, rehabilitation planning, and interpretation of treatment response.

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Clinical Phenomenology of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Neural Substrates of Spatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Spatial neglect is best understood as a network disorder rather than the consequence of damage to a single cortical locus. Acute lesion–symptom mapping and perfusion studies implicate a right-lateralized fronto-parietal–temporal attention system, particularly the inferior parietal lobule, temporo-parietal junction, superior temporal cortex, and ventral frontal regions; importantly, structurally intact cortex may also be functionally compromised by hypoperfusion or diaschisis, helping to explain why neglect can exceed the visible infarct core in the hyperacute stage ref [13], ref [4], ref [5].

Converging evidence further indicates that disconnection of white-matter pathways is central to many neglect syndromes. Tractography and lesion studies have highlighted the superior longitudinal fasciculus, especially fronto-parietal branches linking dorsal and ventral attention systems, as well as other long-range association fibers whose interruption destabilizes spatial orienting and target selection ref [11], ref [6], ref [7]. This disconnection account helps reconcile clinical heterogeneity, since different combinations of cortical and subcortical damage can produce overlapping neglect phenotypes.

Subcortical structures also make important contributions. Thalamic injury can produce neglect, including representational forms, underscoring the role of thalamo-cortical hubs in sustaining spatial representations and attentional priority maps ref [12]. More broadly, models of neglect increasingly emphasize impaired interactions between dorsal orienting mechanisms and ventral reorienting/salience systems, with right-hemisphere lesions causing both hemispatial bias and non-spatial deficits in arousal and sustained attention that aggravate clinical severity ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Clinical Phenomenology of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Representational and Non-Canonical Manifestations
subsections.content:
Beyond the classical bedside picture of ipsilesional orienting bias in peripersonal space, neglect can affect internal representations and other non-canonical spatial codes. Representational neglect is classically demonstrated when patients omit contralesional elements while describing familiar scenes from memory, implying that the disorder can distort spatially organized mental imagery as well as online perception. However, this phenomenon is heterogeneous rather than universal, and dissociations between different forms of imagery-based neglect indicate that representational deficits do not simply mirror perceptual neglect [3].

A related extension concerns neglect within abstract representational spaces, especially number. Patients may show a pathological rightward displacement when bisecting numerical intervals, supporting the influential idea of a spatially organized “mental number line.” Such distortions are not confined to the canonical horizontal axis: displacement has also been reported on a vertical number line in neglect, suggesting that impaired spatial coding can generalize across coordinate frames and task formats [1]. The broader cognitive architecture of numerical representation, including links between magnitude and categorical properties such as parity, further underscores that neglect may interact with distributed, partly spatialized semantic representations rather than only with visual input [2].

Clinically, these non-canonical manifestations matter because they reveal that neglect is not reducible to a unitary sensory-attentional deficit. Instead, patients may present with selective impairments in imagined environments, symbolic sequences, or body- and object-centered transformations, even when standard cancellation or copying tasks incompletely capture the syndrome. Recognition of these variants is important for phenotyping, for interpreting apparent task dissociations, and for designing theory-informed rehabilitation strategies that target representational as well as perceptual-attentional components of neglect [1][3].

subsections.subsection_title: Anosognosia, Awareness, and Social-Cognitive Accounts
subsections.content:
Anosognosia and related disturbances of awareness are important cognitive modulators of spatial neglect because they alter not only symptom report, but also engagement with rehabilitation and the capacity to recruit compensatory strategies. Classical neuropsychological accounts frame anosognosia as a disorder of self-monitoring that can accompany focal brain injury and dissociate across motor, sensory, and cognitive domains, indicating that awareness is not a unitary faculty but a hierarchically organized function ref [17]. After stroke, impaired awareness is common, shows substantial clinical heterogeneity, and is particularly associated with right-hemisphere damage, severe deficits, and poorer functional outcome ref [19].

In neglect syndromes, anosognosia is especially relevant when patients underestimate contralesional deficits or fail to appreciate the functional consequences of their spatial bias. This has encouraged models in which impaired awareness emerges from a mismatch between defective online error signals and preserved premorbid beliefs about bodily competence, rather than from sensory loss alone ref [17], ref [19]. In anosognosia for hemiplegia, social-cognitive and "mentalizing" accounts further suggest that awareness depends partly on mechanisms used to represent one’s own body and action states in relation to others, linking body ownership, perspective taking, and belief updating to disrupted self-knowledge after right-hemisphere lesions ref [18].

These observations are theoretically relevant for neglect because they position awareness at the intersection of attentional control, body representation, and metacognition. They also have practical implications: patients with reduced insight may appear inattentive or noncompliant when the core problem is impaired access to deficit-related information. Although visual-perceptual impairments are also frequent after severe brain injury, including traumatic etiologies, awareness phenomena should be distinguished from primary perceptual disturbance, even when both contribute to functional disability ref [20]. Overall, social-cognitive accounts complement attentional-network models by emphasizing that recovery from neglect depends not only on reorienting space, but also on restoring accurate self-appraisal and error monitoring ref [17], ref [18], ref [19].

subsections.subsection_title: Arousal, Endogenous Control, and Cognitive State Modulation
subsections.content:
Arousal and global attentional state are now recognized as major modulators of neglect severity, complementing lateralized spatial accounts. Robertson and colleagues argued that persistent neglect often includes nonlateralized attentional deficits, particularly reduced sustained attention and impaired alertness, which can amplify contralesional bias and help explain fluctuations across tasks and time ref [21]. Consistent with this view, clinical studies linked neglect to hypoarousal and emotional indifference, suggesting that diminished tonic activation may worsen exploratory behavior and awareness of contralesional space ref [23]. These findings support models in which neglect emerges from an interaction between spatially biased competition and impaired state regulation rather than from a purely directional disorder.

Neglect is also sensitive to endogenous control demands. Manipulating apparent time pressure can alter spatial bias, providing direct evidence that top-down task set and internal response urgency modulate neglect expression ref [22]. More broadly, reduced phasic alerting and deficits of sustained attention have been repeatedly associated with right-hemisphere neglect, and interventions that increase alertness can transiently improve cancellation and visual search performance (e.g., Robertson et al., 1998; Sturm et al., 2006). Such results are important theoretically because they indicate that endogenous control and arousal are not merely epiphenomenal, but can gate the manifestation of spatial deficits.

State dependence is further underscored by pharmacological observations. In stroke patients, administration of the GABAergic sedative midazolam can transiently reinduce previously recovered deficits, including neglect-like symptoms, implying that latent network vulnerabilities may be unmasked when arousal is reduced ref [24]. This has implications for both assessment and treatment: neglect should be sampled across varying cognitive states, and neuromodulatory approaches may be most effective when paired with strategies that optimize vigilance, motivation, and task engagement.

subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Probes, Clinical Variants, and Recovery Dynamics
subsections.content:
Experimental manipulations have been particularly informative for testing causal accounts of neglect. In healthy volunteers, non-invasive brain interference over parietal cortex can induce neglect-like lateralized biases, supporting the view that interhemispheric imbalance and disrupted fronto-parietal control are sufficient to generate core components of spatial asymmetry, even if these models only partially capture the clinical syndrome ref [25]. Converging electrophysiological work further suggests that impaired conscious access in neglect is linked to abnormal fronto-parietal beta/theta synchronization, providing a mechanistic bridge between transient experimental perturbation and lesion-based deficits of awareness ref [29].

Clinical variants also broaden the syndrome beyond the canonical post-stroke presentation. Dissociations across bedside and behavioral measures demonstrate that test sensitivity varies substantially with task demands, implying that apparent absence of neglect may reflect measurement limitations rather than true recovery ref [31]. Neglect can also appear in unusual phenotypes, including personal-care manifestations such as facial shaving neglect and non-stroke neurodegenerative forms such as posterior cortical atrophy, emphasizing that neglect reflects distributed spatial-attentional vulnerability rather than a single disease entity ref [28], ref [30].

Recovery is likewise heterogeneous and dynamic. Longitudinal behavioral analyses show that different neglect components improve at different rates after stroke, with persistent deficits often detectable despite gains on coarse screening measures ref [27]. Case evidence from sequential strokes indicates that recovery trajectories can be reshaped by later lesions, challenging linear models and underscoring the plastic, network-level basis of both symptom expression and remission ref [26]. Together, these findings argue for repeated, multimodal probing of neglect across time, tasks, and clinical contexts rather than relying on a unitary snapshot diagnosis ref [26], ref [27], ref [31].

subsections.subsection_title: Attentional Network Models of Spatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Attentional network models construe spatial neglect not as a unitary sensory loss, but as a disorder of distributed systems that normally allocate, sustain, and reorient attention. Early cueing studies showed that parietal damage selectively impairs covert orienting, particularly disengagement from ipsilesional cues toward contralesional space, establishing a mechanistic link between neglect and disrupted spatial selection ref [33]. Complementing this, work on the right posterior parietal cortex emphasized its role in maintaining attention to locations over time, suggesting that neglect also reflects a failure of sustained spatial priority rather than only defective shifting ref [32].

Network formulations subsequently broadened the account beyond parietal cortex. Mesulam proposed a large-scale attention matrix involving posterior parietal, frontal, and cingulate regions for constructing salience maps and directing behavior toward extrapersonal events ref [36], while Corbetta and Shulman articulated interacting dorsal goal-directed and ventral stimulus-driven attention systems whose imbalance after right-hemisphere injury can produce pathological spatial bias ref [35]. Reviews integrating lesion, neurophysiology, and imaging findings further argue that neglect emerges from dysfunction within fronto-parietal and subcortical circuits rather than from a single cortical locus ref [37], ref [38].

This systems view is supported by acute perfusion imaging, which often demonstrates neglect when structurally spared nodes of the spatial attention network are functionally underperfused, thereby linking symptoms to network-wide physiological failure ref [13]. Subcortical models, including the thalamic reticular 'searchlight' hypothesis, also underscore how thalamic gating may influence selective attentional allocation across cortical territories ref [34]. Clinically, attentional network models therefore frame neglect as a dynamic disorder of interregional coordination, helping explain heterogeneity across patients and motivating treatments that target network rebalancing rather than isolated lesion sites ref [37], ref [38].

subsections.subsection_title: Disconnection and Lesion-Symptom Network Anatomy
subsections.content:
Contemporary accounts increasingly reject a single “neglect center” in favor of a distributed lesion–symptom network model. Meta-analytic lesion evidence shows recurrent involvement of inferior parietal and temporo-parietal cortex, inferior frontal regions, and underlying perisylvian white matter, but also substantial anatomical heterogeneity across patients and task components, arguing against a unitary critical locus ref [39], ref [41]. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping further supports fractionation: perceptual-attentional, exploratory-motor, and representational deficits can map onto partially dissociable cortical and subcortical territories rather than one common lesion site ref [40].

This network view is strengthened by disconnection studies. Classical and modern tractographic work indicates that neglect may arise when fronto-parietal communication is interrupted, particularly through the superior longitudinal fasciculus and related long-range association pathways ref [42], ref [11], ref [46]. Such findings align with primate disconnection models showing that neglect-like behavior can emerge from disrupted interactions between spatial representation systems rather than only from focal cortical destruction ref [43]. Accordingly, white-matter injury helps explain why similar bedside syndromes can follow anatomically distinct strokes.

Lesion-symptom anatomy also extends beyond cortex and white matter to subcortical nodes and remote dysfunction. Neglect after basal ganglia or thalamic lesions has been linked to the putamen, caudate, and pulvinar, implicating subcortical contributions to orienting and network gain control ref [45]. In acute stroke, apparent “subcortical neglect” may partly reflect cortical hypoperfusion and diaschisis within attention networks ref [44], a point presaged by combined structural-functional studies showing that behavioral severity relates not only to lesion topography but also to distributed metabolic dysfunction ref [47]. Overall, neglect is best conceptualized as a disorder of damaged and disconnected attention networks, with lesion location, tract involvement, and remote physiological depression jointly shaping phenotype and recovery.

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Assessment and Rehabilitation Planning
subsections.content:
Clinical guidelines for stroke rehabilitation consistently emphasize that assessment should begin early, be repeated across the care continuum, and directly inform individualized rehabilitation planning. The American Heart Association/American Stroke Association guideline recommends comprehensive interdisciplinary evaluation of neurologic deficits, activity limitations, participation restrictions, comorbidities, mood, cognition, communication, and safety before formulating treatment goals and discharge plans ref [48]. In patients with right-hemisphere stroke, this principle is especially important because visuospatial neglect is often underdetected unless it is explicitly screened during routine rehabilitation intake.

Best-practice guidance further supports standardized assessment using validated measures rather than relying solely on bedside impression. International stroke rehabilitation recommendations call for early identification of impairments that influence mobility, self-care, and community reintegration, with periodic reassessment to capture evolving needs and response to therapy ref [2], ref [3]. For neglect, guideline-concordant planning therefore requires structured neuropsychological or functional testing integrated with occupational and physical therapy evaluations, since neglect substantially worsens disability, fall risk, length of stay, and functional outcome after stroke ref [4], ref [5].

From a rehabilitation-planning perspective, guidelines also favor goal-oriented, task-specific, and multidisciplinary management tailored to the patient’s impairment profile and living context ref [48], ref [2]. This has direct implications for neglect: assessment should distinguish whether deficits primarily affect personal, peripersonal, or extrapersonal space, and whether they co-occur with anosognosia, visual field loss, or motor-intentional deficits, because these features shape treatment selection, caregiver education, and discharge readiness ref [5], ref [6]. Accordingly, neglect assessment is not an ancillary exercise but a core component of evidence-based stroke rehabilitation planning.

subsections.subsection_title: Screening Tools for Post-Stroke Rehabilitation Needs
subsections.content:
Screening for post-stroke rehabilitation needs is intended to identify, as early as possible, patients who require coordinated multidisciplinary intervention and to route them toward an appropriate intensity and setting of care. Validation work on post-stroke rehabilitation guidelines showed that structured screening can be operationalized at the bedside and can improve the consistency with which impairments, activity limitations, and contextual barriers are recognized in routine stroke services ref [49]. In practice, such screening should extend beyond motor deficit to cognition, communication, mood, swallowing, visual function, and participation restrictions, because these domains strongly influence rehabilitation eligibility and timing ref [49], ref [2].

For patients at risk of visuospatial neglect, generic rehabilitation triage is insufficient unless accompanied by focused cognitive-perceptual screening. Neglect is both common and underdetected after right-hemisphere stroke, particularly when clinicians rely only on informal observation or broad neurological scales ref [3], ref [4]. Consensus recommendations therefore favor rapid standardized tools, including cancellation tasks, line bisection, copying, and functional observational measures, to determine whether a patient needs more comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and neglect-specific therapy planning ref [4], ref [5]. The Catherine Bergego Scale is especially useful in rehabilitation screening because it captures neglect as expressed in everyday activities, complementing paper-and-pencil tests that may miss functionally significant deficits ref [6], ref [7].

A pragmatic screening framework for rehabilitation planning should therefore be tiered: an initial service-level screen for overall rehabilitation need, followed by domain-specific instruments for cognition and spatial attention, and then full diagnostic work-up when neglect or other disabling deficits are suspected. This staged approach is consistent with stroke rehabilitation guidance emphasizing early assessment, repeated reassessment across recovery, and linkage between screening findings and individualized treatment goals ref [49], ref [2], ref [5], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostic Evaluation of Spatial Neglect Subtypes
subsections.content:
Diagnostic evaluation of spatial neglect should move beyond a unitary label because neglect comprises partially dissociable deficits across spatial sectors, reference frames, and functional domains. Acute stroke studies show that patients may perform inconsistently across commonly used subtype tests, indicating that no single task adequately captures the syndrome’s heterogeneity and that subtype classification based on one measure is unreliable ref [50]. Accordingly, assessment batteries should sample personal, peripersonal, and extrapersonal space; viewer-, object-, and stimulus-centered coordinates; and perceptual, representational, and motor-exploratory components ref [50], ref [2], ref [3].

Bedside diagnosis usually begins with cancellation, line bisection, copying, drawing, and reading tasks, but these tests are differentially sensitive to egocentric versus allocentric neglect and may under-detect subtle or task-specific impairment. Standardized batteries such as the Behavioural Inattention Test improve breadth, whereas process-based tools such as the Catherine Bergego Scale capture neglect during everyday activities and often reveal disability not evident on paper-and-pencil measures ref [4], ref [5]. Because allocentric neglect can occur without marked egocentric bias, and vice versa, dedicated scoring approaches that separate these dimensions are especially important for treatment planning and prognostication ref [6], ref [7].

A comprehensive diagnostic work-up should also distinguish neglect from visual field loss, extinction, anosognosia, and non-lateralized attentional deficits, while recognizing frequent coexistence. Functional and mechanistic characterization may be refined by computer-based testing and lesion-symptom or network-informed analyses, which link distinct neglect phenotypes to different cortical-subcortical disconnections and may explain variable response to rehabilitation or non-invasive brain stimulation ref [3], ref [8]. In practice, repeated multimodal assessment is preferable to one-time screening, particularly in the acute stage when performance fluctuations can obscure subtype boundaries ref [50], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological Approaches to Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
Pharmacological approaches to visuospatial neglect have largely been motivated by neuromodulatory accounts of attention, arousal, and exploratory behavior. In this framework, catecholaminergic systems are of particular interest because neglect is often exacerbated by reduced alertness and impaired orienting, especially after right-hemisphere stroke. Small experimental and clinical studies therefore suggest that drugs acting on noradrenergic or dopaminergic transmission may transiently enhance contralesional exploration or improve performance on cancellation and visual search tasks, although the evidence base remains limited and heterogeneous ref [51], ref [52].

Noradrenergic manipulation has shown some of the clearest proof-of-concept effects. In particular, studies of noradrenergic enhancement reported improved spatial exploration in patients with visual neglect, consistent with the view that boosting tonic and phasic alerting can partially rebalance attentional deployment toward neglected space ref [51]. Related work on alertness training and the close linkage between arousal networks and neglect also supports the plausibility of this mechanism, even if medication effects have not yet translated into a standardized treatment pathway ref [3], ref [4].

Dopaminergic strategies have likewise been explored on the premise that fronto-striatal dysfunction may contribute to reduced initiation, exploratory drive, and sustained attention in neglect. A case series using carbidopa/levodopa described behavioral improvement in left neglect after stroke ref [52], and other small studies of dopaminergic agonists have reported benefits in selected patients ref [5], ref [6]. However, pharmacological trials remain few, typically underpowered, and variable in lesion profile, chronicity, and outcome measures; moreover, some patients improve while others do not, implying strong dependence on underlying anatomy and cognitive phenotype ref [6], ref [7]. At present, drug therapy should therefore be regarded as adjunctive and individualized rather than established routine care ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.subsection_title: Non-invasive Brain Stimulation for Therapeutic Recovery
subsections.content:
Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) has emerged as a theory-driven adjunct for visuospatial neglect rehabilitation, motivated largely by interhemispheric competition models in which right-hemisphere damage produces relative hyperexcitability of the intact left parietal cortex. Accordingly, therapeutic protocols have aimed either to downregulate the contralesional hemisphere with low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) or inhibitory theta-burst stimulation, or to upregulate residual activity in damaged right fronto-parietal networks with anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) ref [53]. Across studies, the strongest signals have typically been reported for parietal stimulation, especially when NIBS is paired with conventional visuospatial training rather than delivered as a stand-alone intervention ref [53].

The clinical evidence remains encouraging but heterogeneous. Reviews specific to neglect suggest short-term improvements on cancellation, line bisection, and exploratory tasks after inhibitory stimulation of the left posterior parietal cortex, although sample sizes are small and protocols vary substantially in target, intensity, and treatment dose ref [53]. Broader stroke evidence indicates that tDCS can modestly improve activities of daily living and some motor or cognitive outcomes, but certainty is limited by risk of bias and inconsistency, making extrapolation to neglect-specific recovery cautious ref [54]. More generally, work on chronic stroke has shown that stimulation effects are state-dependent and often enhanced when coupled to active training, a principle that is highly relevant for neglect rehabilitation design ref [55].

Current interpretation therefore favors NIBS as an adjunctive, network-oriented intervention rather than a universally effective therapy. Key unresolved issues include patient selection, chronicity, lesion topology, durability of benefit, and the choice between inhibitory versus facilitatory approaches. Future trials should use sham-controlled designs, functionally meaningful endpoints, and mechanistically informed targeting to determine whether stimulation-induced gains generalize beyond paper-and-pencil measures to sustained improvements in daily spatial behavior ref [53], ref [54].

subsections.subsection_title: Assessment and Outcome Considerations in Treatment Studies
subsections.content:
A central challenge in treatment studies of visuospatial neglect is that outcome depends strongly on how neglect is measured. Brief screening tools such as line bisection, cancellation, copying, and drawing tasks are useful for case detection, but they sample partially distinct components of neglect and can miss mild, object-centered, personal, or context-dependent deficits; consequently, reliance on a single bedside test risks underestimating treatment effects or falsely concluding recovery ref [56]. Contemporary trials therefore benefit from multi-component batteries that combine conventional paper-and-pencil screening with functional measures and, where possible, assessments sensitive to sustained attention and non-lateralized deficits that commonly co-occur with neglect.

Methodological reviews have emphasized that the relationship between neglect and post-stroke disability is highly sensitive to outcome definition, timing of assessment, and whether disability is indexed by impairment-level tests or by activities of daily living ref [57]. Functional scales such as the Catherine Bergego Scale were developed precisely because laboratory improvement does not necessarily translate into better everyday exploration, wheelchair navigation, dressing, or eating; accordingly, treatment studies should distinguish impairment reduction from ecologically meaningful benefit. Repeated assessments across acute, subacute, and chronic phases are also important, since spontaneous recovery, practice effects, and fluctuating arousal can confound interpretation of intervention efficacy ref [57].

For therapeutic trials, best practice is thus to predefine primary endpoints, include both impairment-based and functional outcomes, and document lesion chronicity, neglect subtype, and co-occurring anosognosia or hemianopia as potential modifiers of response. Such stratification is particularly relevant for pharmacological and non-invasive brain stimulation studies, where modest average effects may conceal clinically important benefits in specific phenotypes. Standardized reporting of baseline severity and responder analyses should improve comparability across studies and strengthen meta-analytic synthesis ref [56], ref [57].

subsections.subsection_title: Neuroanatomical Factors Shaping Intervention Response
subsections.content:
Intervention response in visuospatial neglect is strongly constrained by lesion topology and by the integrity of distributed attention networks. Longitudinal lesion-behaviour work indicates that the anatomical substrates of acute neglect are not identical to those sustaining chronic symptoms, with early deficits more closely linked to widespread right-hemisphere damage and later persistence more specifically associated with damage to temporo-parietal and frontal white-matter pathways ref [58]. This distinction is clinically important because treatments delivered in the acute phase may act on partially dysfunctional but structurally preserved networks, whereas chronic non-response may reflect irreversible disconnection.

Converging evidence from structural mapping studies further suggests that neglect severity and chronicity are shaped not only by cortical injury but also by disconnection of fronto-parietal and temporo-frontal association tracts, especially the superior longitudinal fasciculus and related perisylvian pathways ref [2], ref [3]. Damage involving the inferior parietal lobule, superior temporal cortex, insula, and ventral frontal regions has been repeatedly implicated, supporting network-based rather than single-locus accounts ref [4], ref [5]. Such heterogeneity likely explains why the same intervention—for example prism adaptation or non-invasive brain stimulation—produces marked benefit in some patients but limited change in others.

These neuroanatomical considerations have direct implications for treatment stratification. Patients with preserved interhemispheric and dorsal attention network connectivity may be more amenable to therapies that rebalance cortical excitability, whereas extensive white-matter disconnection or involvement of subcortical hubs may limit generalization beyond task-specific gains ref [3], ref [6]. Accordingly, treatment studies should incorporate lesion location, tract damage, and chronicity as moderators, ideally combining behavioural outcomes with structural and functional imaging to identify responders and to align intervention choice with the underlying neural architecture of neglect ref [58], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Evidence Base and Methods
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Foundations of Interhemispheric Balance in Spatial Attention
subsections.content:
The dominant theoretical framework for spatial attention posits that orienting emerges from a dynamic balance between homologous frontoparietal systems in the two hemispheres. In Kinsbourne’s hemispheric rivalry account, each hemisphere directs attention contralaterally while exerting reciprocal inhibition over its counterpart; spatial bias therefore reflects the moment-to-moment equilibrium of this competitive interaction. Contemporary formulations refine this view by emphasizing flexible priority maps within dorsal attention cortex, particularly the posterior parietal cortices, whose imbalance can shift attentional weights across space ref [61].

Causal perturbation studies in healthy participants strongly support this model. Applying inhibitory or excitatory non-invasive stimulation over one parietal cortex produces predictable, bidirectional changes in spatial judgments, consistent with release from interhemispheric inhibition or enhancement of contralateral competitive drive ref [60]. Combined rTMS-fMRI work further shows that transient disruption of one parietal node induces remote changes in the contralateral hemisphere and associated attentional networks, indicating that the two hemispheres function as a coupled system rather than independent processors ref [59]. Such findings provide a mechanistic bridge between transient experimentally induced spatial biases and the pathological neglect that follows unilateral stroke.

This framework also helps explain why age and brain damage can alter lateralization patterns relevant to rehabilitation. The HAROLD model, although developed primarily in cognitive aging, suggests that reduced hemispheric asymmetry may reflect compensatory recruitment under conditions of neural inefficiency or damage ref [62]. In spatial attention, this implies that therapeutic neuromodulation should not only suppress pathological hyperexcitability in the intact hemisphere but also consider adaptive bilateral reorganization. Accordingly, interhemispheric balance theory has become the conceptual basis for stimulation strategies designed either to downregulate the contralesional hemisphere or to restore more physiological bilateral network interactions in neglect.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Evidence Base and Methods
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Perturbation of Parietal Attention Networks in Healthy Participants
subsections.content:
Experimental perturbation studies in healthy participants have been central to testing causal models of spatial attention and, in particular, the interhemispheric competition account. Transient disruption of the right posterior parietal cortex (PPC) with theta-burst stimulation can induce neglect-like exploration biases, shifting visual sampling rightward and reducing attention to left hemispace, thereby reproducing key behavioral features of clinical neglect in attenuated form ref [63]. Complementing this, bilateral TBS protocols have shown that manipulating the relative excitability of the two parietal cortices alters overt attentional orienting in a direction consistent with interhemispheric balance models ref [66].

Convergent evidence comes from tDCS studies targeting PPC. Polarizing stimulation over parietal cortex has been shown to bias perceived visual position and visuospatial localization in healthy observers, indicating that even weak tonic shifts in cortical excitability can recalibrate spatial representations ref [64], ref [65]. These findings are important because they suggest that parietal stimulation does not merely affect motor responses or search strategies, but can influence the underlying coding of egocentric spatial coordinates.

Taken together, perturbation experiments in neurologically intact individuals provide a mechanistic bridge between theory and rehabilitation. They demonstrate that lateralized changes in PPC excitability are sufficient to generate predictable spatial biases, lending causal support to models later invoked to explain neglect after stroke and to justify inhibitory stimulation of the contralesional hemisphere or facilitatory stimulation of ipsilesional networks in therapeutic protocols ref [63], ref [66].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Evidence Base and Methods
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiology and Network Mechanisms of Spatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Spatial neglect is increasingly understood as a disorder of large-scale attention networks rather than a purely focal syndrome of the right inferior parietal lobe. Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection studies indicate that neglect commonly follows damage affecting a right-lateralized fronto-parietal-insular network and its white-matter links, particularly the superior longitudinal fasciculus, thereby disrupting interactions between dorsal orienting and ventral salience/reorienting systems ref [4], ref [5], ref [6]. This network perspective helps explain why similar behavioral phenotypes can arise from cortical, subcortical, or tract lesions.

A complementary mechanistic account emphasizes pathological interhemispheric imbalance. Following right-hemisphere injury, the intact left hemisphere may become relatively hyperexcitable, exerting excessive inhibitory influence over damaged right parietal systems and biasing attention ipsilesionally. Neurophysiological evidence supports this model, including hyperexcitability of parietal-motor functional connections in the intact left hemisphere of neglect patients ref [67]. Functional studies further suggest that impaired conscious perception in neglect is linked to abnormal long-range oscillatory coordination: synchronization of fronto-parietal beta and theta networks has been identified as a signature of visual awareness, implying that neglect reflects a failure to establish the distributed temporal dynamics required for awareness of contralesional stimuli ref [29].

These findings converge on the view that neglect is a disconnection and dysrhythmia syndrome, in which structural damage, altered interhemispheric competition, and disrupted oscillatory coupling jointly degrade spatial representations and attentional selection. This framework has direct therapeutic implications, because non-invasive stimulation can be used to suppress maladaptive hyperactivity, enhance residual right-hemisphere processing, or entrain network rhythms; frequency-specific approaches such as transcranial alternating current stimulation are conceptually aligned with this network-restorative logic ref [68], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Evidence Base and Methods
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic rTMS and Theta-Burst Stimulation for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Therapeutic rTMS and theta-burst stimulation (TBS) for visuospatial neglect have largely been developed from the interhemispheric rivalry model, with most protocols aiming to downregulate the intact left posterior parietal cortex and thereby reduce pathological hyperexcitability that may suppress residual right-hemisphere attention networks. Early proof-of-concept studies showed that inhibitory stimulation of the unaffected hemisphere could transiently ameliorate neglect or extinction, including low-frequency rTMS over left parietal or frontal regions in right-brain-damaged patients ref [70], ref [71], ref [73].

Subsequent clinical studies suggested that repeated inhibitory stimulation may produce effects extending beyond the immediate post-stimulation window. Low-frequency rTMS over the unaffected posterior parietal cortex was associated with both short-term behavioral gains and longer-lasting improvement in some cohorts, and randomized evidence in acute stroke further supported beneficial effects on neglect severity ref [72], ref [76]. Open-label pilot work also indicated feasibility in post-stroke populations, although sample sizes were small and outcome measures heterogeneous ref [12].

TBS protocols were introduced to increase efficiency and potentially strengthen cumulative plasticity. Repeated parietal theta-burst trains were reported to induce long-lasting improvement after even a single session in selected patients ref [69], while later studies found that continuous or intermittent TBS could improve neglect symptoms, activities of daily living, and resting-state connectivity within attention networks ref [74], ref [75], ref [77], ref [78]. Overall, the literature supports inhibitory stimulation of the contralesional hemisphere as a promising adjunct to rehabilitation, but it remains limited by modest samples, variable timing after stroke, and inconsistent stimulation parameters.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Evidence Base and Methods
subsections.subsection_title: tDCS-Based Rehabilitation Approaches for Neglect
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been explored in neglect rehabilitation as a low-intensity neuromodulatory approach intended to rebalance pathological interhemispheric asymmetry after right-hemisphere stroke. In this framework, anodal stimulation is used to facilitate damaged right parietal-attentional regions, cathodal stimulation to suppress relatively hyperactive left parietal cortex, or both poles are combined in biparietal montages. Early clinical work suggested that tDCS can reduce neglect severity on cancellation, line bisection, and functional spatial tasks, although effects were generally modest and heterogeneous across patients and outcome measures ref [80].

The small but conceptually important intervention literature indicates that tDCS may be most useful when embedded within active rehabilitation rather than delivered in isolation. A single-case report using biparietal tDCS combined with cognitive training described improvement consistent with the interhemispheric rebalance model, while also highlighting the feasibility of pairing stimulation with task-specific attentional practice ref [81]. Similarly, a pilot randomized trial in subacute stroke found that combining tDCS with feedback-based training yielded greater gains than behavioral training alone on neglect-related outcomes, supporting the idea that stimulation may act as an adjunct that enhances training-dependent plasticity ref [82].

Overall, the tDCS evidence base for visuospatial neglect remains preliminary: studies are few, samples are small, stimulation parameters vary, and durability and functional generalization are insufficiently established. Nonetheless, current findings support continued evaluation of individualized montages, repeated-session protocols, and combination approaches that integrate tDCS with visuomotor, feedback, or cognitive training paradigms, ideally in adequately powered sham-controlled trials stratified by lesion location and neglect subtype ref [80], ref [81], ref [82].
